front: Bow, stern, port, starboard — what does each mean?
note: The four words every order on deck depends on; already at beginner level.

front: Amidships
note: One-line positional vocabulary, given as an order ('fender amidships').

front: Beam (two meanings)
note: Both meanings are plain vocabulary and the direction sense is needed to report a sighting.

front: Draught
note: Single-sentence definition, no calculation, no tide.

front: Air draught
note: Plain definition; a crew member hears it under bridges and needs no theory for it.

front: Freeboard
note: One-line hull vocabulary.

front: Windward and leeward
note: Core crew vocabulary; the 'leeward is the boom's side' cue is exactly the beginner's handle.

front: Lee shore — and why it matters
note: The danger/shelter framing is a skipper's anchorage decision. CC card: a lee shore is simply land the wind is blowing onto, a weather shore is land the wind blows off — no shelter judgement.

front: Ahead, astern, abeam, abaft, forward of the beam
note: The relative-direction set a crew member needs to report what they see to the skipper.

front: Which direction is 22.5° abaft the beam, and why does the number matter?
note: Exists only to explain sidelight arcs and the overtaking sector — navigation lights and IRPCS, both hard exclusions.

front: Heel versus list
note: Two short definitions; reassuring and useful to a first-timer on their first heel.

front: The three rotational motions of a boat at sea
note: Roll/pitch/yaw is plain vocabulary and feeds straight into seasickness and helming.

front: Displacement
note: Hull-speed formula; naval architecture a crew member is never given as an order.

front: What makes a cruising yacht stable?
note: Centre of buoyancy, righting moment and angle of vanishing stability are theory. CC card: the heavy keel keeps her upright, so heeling is normal and she will not tip over.

front: Reserve buoyancy
note: Only the practical tail matters at crew level. CC card: keep hatches and washboards shut at sea so water cannot get below.

front: What happens to stability if you fill the water tanks and load the anchor locker?
note: Free-surface effect and loading decisions are the skipper's. CC card: stow heavy gear low and aft of the bow, and never leave gear loose on deck or on the coachroof.

front: Name the three sides and three corners of a mainsail.
note: Pure sail vocabulary; the syllabus names luff/leech/foot/head/tack/clew explicitly.

front: Standing rigging versus running rigging
note: 'Rigging and sails' is half the CC section-1 title; this is the naming card for it.

front: Halyard versus sheet
note: The single most order-driven distinction on the boat, in one line.

front: Kicker (boom vang) — what does it do?
note: Leech tension and sail twist are theory a first-timer does not have. CC card: the kicker holds the boom down; you will be asked to tension or ease it.

front: Topping lift
note: One sentence, and 'take up the topping lift' is a literal crew order when dropping the main.

front: Genoa versus jib
note: Headsail naming plus furling; no theory.

front: What is a seacock and why must you know where they all are?
note: Flooding-defence framing and softwood bungs are skipper-level. CC card: a seacock is the valve on a hole through the hull — know where the heads and sink ones are and leave them as the skipper set them.

front: Bilge, sole, bulkhead
note: Three below-decks words, one line each.

front: Pulpit, pushpit, stanchions, guardrails, jackstay
note: Deck-fitting names a crew member is told to clip to or move along.

front: Warp, spring, breast line
note: 'Handling warps' is a named CC ropework bullet; this is the naming card and requires no decision.

front: What is a transit?
note: Pilotage tool — position lines and clearing transits are a hard exclusion.

front: Cable (as a unit)
note: A chartwork distance unit; the second sense belongs to anchoring, which is not a CC section.

front: Fathom
note: Chart depth units — chartwork.

front: Fenders, fairleads, cleats and bollards
note: CC ropework names cleats and single and double bollards outright; fendering is a general duty on arrival.

front: Keel types and what each means for you
note: Drying out, directional stability and windward performance are boat-choice and skipper knowledge.

front: What does 'make fast', 'belay', 'surge' and 'snub' mean?
note: These four words are literally orders shouted at crew; nothing here has to be decided.

front: Riding turn
note: Winch handling is a named CC bullet, and the rolling-hitch fix is the 'correct use' of a CC-named knot.

front: Chafe — why is it the thing that actually breaks mooring lines?
note: Framed as a skipper's insight about overnight failure. CC card: lines wear where they rub, so lead every warp through a fairlead and never over a sharp edge.

front: Figure of eight — use
note: Named CC knot with its correct use, in one sentence.

front: Bowline — use
note: Named CC knot; the uses listed are all crew jobs.

front: Clove hitch — use and limitation
note: Named CC knot; the fender-lanyard use and the slipping caveat are exactly what a beginner must know.

front: Round turn and two half hitches — use
note: Named CC knot with its correct use.

front: Rolling hitch — use
note: Named CC knot; the riding-turn use is the standard teaching example.

front: Reef knot — correct use and the trap
note: Named CC knot; the 'not for joining two ropes' trap is the point of the CC knot-use requirement.

front: Sheet bend and double sheet bend
note: Both named in the CC knot list, with the single/double distinction the syllabus asks for.

front: Which knot for a jib sheet to the clew of a headsail?
note: A knot-use recall card on a job crew are given directly.

front: What are the three parts of a rope you name when tying knots?
note: The vocabulary an instructor uses while teaching the knots; the bitter-end aside is one clause and harmless.

front: Polyester (Terylene / Dacron) — properties and use
note: Rope material properties are explicitly Day Skipper ropework, not CC.

front: Nylon (polyamide) — properties and use
note: Rope material properties — DS only.

front: Polypropylene — properties and use
note: Rope material properties — DS only.

front: Aramid and HMPE (Dyneema, Spectra) — properties and use
note: High-end rope specification; well beyond a first-timer and not a CC bullet.

front: Why whip or heat-seal a rope's end?
note: Rope maintenance; CC ropework is coiling, stowing, securing, warps and knots only.

front: How much strength does a knot cost you?
note: Breaking-strain theory and splicing; nothing a crew member is ordered to do.

front: Care of synthetic rope
note: 'Retire it when the core is glazed' is a condemnation decision. CC card: rinse and dry ropes, stow them coiled out of the sun, and never stand on a rope.

front: How do you coil rope so it runs cleanly?
note: Coiling is a named CC bullet and the laid-vs-braided distinction is a hands-on instruction, not theory.

front: Which knot takes the load off a jammed, loaded sheet?
note: Rolling-hitch correct-use recall; the crew is told to do exactly this.

front: How do you choose an anchorage?
note: Anchoring as skipper — a forecast-and-tide decision, hard exclusion.

front: How much scope do you let out?
note: Scope calculation from height of tide; anchoring and tides both excluded.

front: What depth do you use to work out scope?
note: Charted depth plus height of tide — tidal calculation.

front: Good and bad holding ground
note: Chart seabed abbreviations; chartwork plus an anchoring decision.

front: Describe the anchoring drill.
note: The skipper's drill, including boat handling and signals.

front: Why lower the anchor rather than throw it, and why with the boat moving astern?
note: Anchoring technique and its rationale; not a CC section.

front: How do you check the anchor is holding?
note: Transits and bearings — pilotage plus an anchoring judgement.

front: Signals for a vessel at anchor
note: Navigation lights and day shapes — hard exclusion.

front: Sound signal for a vessel at anchor in restricted visibility
note: Sound signals — hard exclusion.

front: How do you weigh anchor?
note: Anchoring evolution run by the skipper; not a CC section even though crew assist.

front: The anchor is fouled and will not come up — what can you do?
note: Problem-solving decision under anchoring.

front: CQR or plough anchor
note: Ground-tackle selection; anchoring is not a CC section.

front: Danforth or Fortress anchor
note: Ground-tackle selection.

front: Bruce or claw anchor
note: Ground-tackle selection.

front: Modern scoop anchors (Rocna, Spade, Vulcan, Excel)
note: Ground-tackle selection.

front: Fisherman anchor
note: Ground-tackle selection.

front: Why is chain better than rope for anchoring?
note: Catenary theory under anchoring.

front: What is a swinging circle and how big is it?
note: Anchoring geometry at all states of tide.

front: Anchoring in a strong tidal stream with a wind against it
note: Tidal concept plus an anchoring decision.

front: Why keep an anchor watch?
note: Anchor watch is set and judged by the skipper; the CC watchkeeping bullet is general duties underway, not this.

front: What is a kedge anchor for?
note: Kedging off after grounding — squarely skipper work.

front: What safety brief should every new crew member get before you leave?
note: Written from the skipper's side and includes sending a VHF distress alert. CC card: what to make sure you have been shown on day one — lifejacket, clipping points, extinguishers and blanket, liferaft, heads, seacocks, MOB shout.

front: Lifejacket or buoyancy aid: what is the difference, and what rating do you want for cruising?
note: Lifejacket vs buoyancy aid, newtons and crotch strap are precisely the CC section-5 bar; nothing here is a decision the crew makes.

front: When should the crew wear lifejackets and harnesses?
note: Answer opens 'whenever the skipper says so' — the CC compliance bullet stated as an order.

front: What is a danbuoy for?
note: Throwing the danbuoy is the crew's immediate MOB action, which the syllabus says is directly reusable.

front: Red parachute rocket flare, red hand flare, orange smoke, white flare — what is each for?
note: 'Knows when they should be used' is the CC bullet verbatim; same depth in both syllabi.

front: How do you fire a hand flare, and how do you fire a parachute rocket?
note: 'Can operate distress flares' is an assessed CC skill; this is the operating instruction, not a decision.

front: What fire extinguishers should a cruising yacht carry, and where?
note: Equipping the boat and checking service dates is the owner's job. CC card: find the extinguishers and the fire blanket on your boat before you sail, and know which one is the galley blanket.

front: How do you fight a galley fat fire?
note: Galley duty plus 'action to be taken in the event of fire'; three plain instructions.

front: How do you fight an engine compartment fire?
note: Assumes access to fuel shut-off and a dedicated extinguisher port. CC card: if the engine bay is alight, do not open it — opening it feeds the fire; shout for the skipper and stay clear.

front: The four elements of fire prevention on a yacht
note: Ends in seasonal installation checks. CC card: the everyday habits — gas off at the bottle, never leave the cooker, no naked flame while fuelling, keep the bilge free of oily rags.

front: Why is LPG particularly dangerous on a boat, and how is the risk managed?
note: Locker drains, bubble testers and hose dates are installation detail. CC card: gas is heavier than air so a leak sinks into the bilge and cannot blow away — always turn the gas off at the bottle when you finish cooking.

front: What goes in a grab bag? Name eight items.
note: A recall list, not a judgement; sits directly under the liferaft bullet.

front: When do you actually get into the liferaft?
note: 'Step up into it' is the standard CC teaching line and needs no theory.

front: How do you launch and board a liferaft?
note: Matches the CC bullet word for word; a sequence of physical actions.

front: What is a radar reflector for and why does it matter in fog?
note: Being seen on radar in poor visibility is not in any CC bullet; it belongs with the restricted-visibility material.

front: EPIRB versus PLB versus SART versus AIS beacon
note: A four-way comparison of kit a crew member never operates. CC card: one line — the boat carries a distress beacon that tells rescuers where you are; know where it is stowed.

front: What lifesaving gear should you check before every passage?
note: Preparation for sea as skipper — service dates, in-date flares, hydrostatic release; a hard exclusion.

front: How do you deal with a crew member who is seriously seasick?
note: Written as the skipper managing a casualty. CC card: what to do when you feel sick — stay on deck, low and warm, eyes on the horizon, eat something, take the helm, take tablets before you sail.

front: Cold water shock — what happens and what do you do?
note: Half the card is rescuer technique (horizontal recovery, post-immersion collapse). CC card: the casualty side only — cold water makes you gasp and lose grip, so float on your back for the first 60-90 seconds until it passes.

front: Hypothermia — the signs and the treatment
note: First-aid treatment of a casualty; CC's newer wording covers cold water shock only.

front: What is a jackstay and how should a tether be used?
note: Harness, tether and clipping-on rules are the CC bullet; every instruction here is given as an order.

front: Minimum first aid you should be able to do at sea
note: First aid is not a CC section, and the card ends in a PAN-PAN VHF call.

front: Are flares a legal requirement, and what are the modern alternatives?
note: Carriage law, MMSI registration and disposal — owner's problem, not the crew's.

front: What is a hydrostatic release unit and why does the liferaft need one?
note: Stowage and servicing of the raft cradle; the CC bullet stops at launching and boarding.

front: What does IRPCS stand for, and do they apply to a small yacht?
note: CC section 9 is one line about lookout; naming the regulations starts the deck down the rule-by-rule road.

front: Rule 2 — the responsibility rule
note: Names a rule number; IRPCS steering and sailing rules are a hard exclusion.

front: Rule 5 — look-out
note: Right topic, wrong register — it quotes rule text. CC card: what keeping a lookout actually means — scan all round including astern and to leeward behind the genoa, and report what you see to the skipper.

front: Rule 6 — safe speed. What determines it?
note: A skipper's judgement, radar included.

front: Rule 7 — how do you know there is a risk of collision?
note: Constant bearing is the one concept a lookout needs, but this card carries a rule number, radar and tows. CC card: if another boat's bearing stays the same as she gets closer, you are on a collision course — tell the skipper.

front: Rule 8 — what must action to avoid collision be like?
note: Avoiding action is the skipper's decision.

front: Rule 9 — narrow channels
note: Rule number and a navigation decision.

front: Rule 10: how do you use a traffic separation scheme, and what applies if you have to cross one?
note: Passage planning and TSS crossing — well beyond CC.

front: Rule 12 — two sailing vessels approaching
note: Give-way and stand-on between sailing vessels — explicitly excluded.

front: Which side is the windward side for the purposes of Rule 12?
note: A definition that exists only to apply Rule 12.

front: Rule 13 — overtaking
note: Steering and sailing rule with sector geometry.

front: Rule 14 — head-on situation
note: Steering and sailing rule.

front: Rule 15 — crossing situation
note: Steering and sailing rule.

front: Rule 16 — the give-way vessel's duty
note: Give-way duty; the crew never makes this call.

front: Rule 17 — the stand-on vessel's duty
note: Stand-on duty; a skipper's decision under pressure.

front: Rule 18 — the order of responsibilities between vessels
note: The full hierarchy — the deepest IRPCS card in the file.

front: A yacht under sail with the engine running in gear meets a motor cruiser — who gives way?
note: A three-rule scenario requiring a decision.

front: What day shape should a sailing vessel motor-sailing show?
note: Day shapes — hard exclusion.

front: Rule 19: who does it apply to, and what four things does it require of you?
note: Restricted visibility conduct — skipper and radar.

front: Rule 19 — which alterations should you avoid?
note: Radar-only avoiding action.

front: Rule 19 — what must you do if you hear a fog signal forward of your beam?
note: Sound signals plus a conduct decision in fog.

front: Rule 20 — when must lights be shown?
note: Navigation lights — hard exclusion.

front: Rule 3 — what is a 'vessel not under command'?
note: A Rule 18 hierarchy definition.

front: Rule 3 — what is a 'vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre'?
note: A Rule 18 hierarchy definition with a long deemed-to-include list.

front: Rule 3 — what is a 'vessel engaged in fishing'?
note: A Rule 18 hierarchy definition.

front: Rule 3 — what is meant by 'restricted visibility'?
note: Definition serving Rule 19.

front: Rule 3 — 'underway' versus 'making way'
note: The distinction is useful vocabulary but this card cites Rule 3 and justifies itself by lights and fog signals. CC card: underway simply means not tied up, not anchored and not aground — you can be underway and still drifting.

front: A large ship is approaching in a narrow buoyed channel and you are under sail in a 10 m yacht. What do you do?
note: Cites Rule 9 and asks the crew to decide. CC card: a big ship in a channel cannot stop or turn for you — if you see one from the foredeck, tell the skipper straight away.

front: What does five or more short and rapid blasts mean, and what should you do on hearing them?
note: Sound signals plus a give-way decision — doubly excluded.

front: You are the stand-on vessel and the other vessel is doing nothing. What is your legal position?
note: Rule 17 judgement.

front: Two power-driven vessels crossing: A has B on her port bow. What must A do?
note: Crossing-rule geometry exercise.

front: What is the difference between the international rules and local harbour rules?
note: Almanac and byelaw research before arrival — skipper's passage preparation.

front: What does 'shall not impede' actually oblige you to do?
note: Rule 8(f) legal nuance.

front: Rule 11 — when do Rules 12 to 18 apply at all?
note: Scope rule for the whole excluded block.

front: You are under sail, overtaking a motor cruiser. Who keeps clear?
note: Rule 13 overriding Rule 18 — the most rule-lawyerly card in the section.

front: Define masthead light, sidelights, sternlight and all-round light with their arcs.
note: Navigation lights — hard exclusion.

front: What lights does a power-driven vessel under 50 m show when underway?
note: Navigation lights.

front: What extra light does a power-driven vessel of 50 m or more show?
note: Navigation lights.

front: What lights does a sailing vessel under sail show?
note: Navigation lights.

front: Why must you not use a masthead tricolour and deck-level sidelights at the same time?
note: Navigation lights.

front: What lights may a sailing vessel under 7 m, or a vessel under oars, show?
note: Navigation lights; the tender link is incidental and rule-cited.

front: What lights does a vessel at anchor show?
note: Navigation lights and day shapes.

front: What lights and shapes does a vessel aground show?
note: Navigation lights and day shapes.

front: What lights and shapes does a vessel not under command show?
note: Navigation lights and day shapes.

front: What lights and shapes does a vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre show?
note: Navigation lights and day shapes.

front: What lights and shape does a vessel constrained by her draught show?
note: Navigation lights and day shapes.

front: What lights and shape does a trawler show?
note: Navigation lights and day shapes.

front: What lights does a vessel fishing other than trawling show?
note: Navigation lights and day shapes.

front: What lights does a vessel towing show, and what changes once the tow exceeds 200 m?
note: Navigation lights and towing — both excluded.

front: What lights does a pilot vessel on duty show?
note: Navigation lights.

front: What lights and shape does a vessel engaged in dredging or underwater operations show?
note: Navigation lights and day shapes.

front: What lights does a vessel engaged in minesweeping show?
note: Navigation lights and day shapes.

front: What lights does a hovercraft in non-displacement mode show?
note: Navigation lights.

front: You see a red light and a green light and a white light above and between them, all steady. What is it and what do you do?
note: Light recognition plus a Rule 14 decision.

front: You see only a green light and a white masthead light. What are you looking at?
note: Light recognition.

front: You see only a red light and a white masthead light. What are you looking at, and what must you do?
note: Light recognition plus a give-way decision.

front: You see a single white light and nothing else. Name four things it could be.
note: Light recognition; night cruising is not a CC competence.

front: You see two white lights in a vertical line, the higher one to the right of the lower. What is it doing?
note: Light recognition and aspect.

front: Sector lights — what are they for?
note: Light characteristics and pilotage.

front: Leading lights
note: Pilotage — leading lines.

front: A directional light
note: Pilotage.

front: What is the difference between the range of a light and its visibility to you?
note: Nominal, luminous and geographical range — chartwork theory.

front: What is 'loom' and 'rising' or 'dipping' a light?
note: Dipping distance gives a position line — navigation.

front: How far must navigation lights be visible, by vessel length?
note: Rule 22 table.

front: What lights must a yacht show at night when motor-sailing?
note: Navigation lights and day shapes.

front: What does a small vessel engaged in diving operations show?
note: Navigation lights and shapes.

front: Which lights and shapes is a small vessel excused from showing?
note: Navigation lights and shapes exemptions.

front: Define a short blast and a prolonged blast.
note: Sound signals — hard exclusion.

front: What do one, two and three short blasts mean?
note: Manoeuvring signals.

front: What do five or more short and rapid blasts mean?
note: Sound signals.

front: In a narrow channel, what signal means 'I intend to overtake you on your starboard side'?
note: Sound signals plus narrow channels.

front: What signal do you sound when approaching a bend where other vessels may be hidden?
note: Sound signals.

front: Fog signal — power-driven vessel making way through the water
note: Fog signals.

front: Fog signal — power-driven vessel underway but stopped and making no way
note: Fog signals.

front: Fog signal — sailing vessel underway
note: Fog signals.

front: Fog signal — vessel at anchor
note: Fog signals.

front: Fog signal — vessel aground
note: Fog signals.

front: Fog signal — vessel being towed
note: Fog signals and towing.

front: What are the sound signalling requirements for a vessel of less than 12 m?
note: Rule 33 carriage requirements.

front: Fog signal — pilot vessel on duty
note: Fog signals.

front: Rule 36 — what may you do to attract attention?
note: Names a rule number; a skipper's collision-avoidance action.

front: What sound signal accompanies a distress situation?
note: Annex IV distress signals; CC emergency equipment stops at flares and the liferaft.

front: What sound signalling equipment must a vessel carry?
note: Rule 33 carriage requirements.

front: May manoeuvring signals be made with a light?
note: Rule 34(b) manoeuvring signals.
